notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to our 4 week Cross Training Plan for Injured Runners

It is extremely frustrating being injured and not being able to run. Your fitness level, strength, diet, and mental health all usually suffer when you can’t run.

If you have an injury that requires some rest from running, there are almost always some cross-training options available to help you maintain your fitness, strength, and sanity.

By cross-training while you are injured, and including some simple strength, stretching and foam rolling routines, you will speed up your recovery time and ultimately make your return to running easier and more successful.

Before you get started, you need to work out which cross training methods are the most suitable for your particular injury

What cross-training option will work best for you?

First, you need to classify your injury.

The type of cross-training you will get the most benefit from while you are injured depends on the nature of your injury. Not all cross-training methods are appropriate for all injuries. For example, cycling can make ITB injuries worse.

Decide which of these categories your injury falls into:

- Hip/Lower Back/Glute/ Hamstring

- Knee / ITB

- Foot / Ankle / Shin / Plantar Fascia / Calf

Everyone’s particular injury will be slightly different, so you need to “listen to your body” and work out which cross-training methods are going to work for you, and which ones won’t.

If it feels like a particular type of training session is aggravating your pain, then you need to adjust accordingly. That might mean reducing the resistance on an exercise bike or ellipitical machine for example, it might mean reducing the training time, or it might mean you need to choose a different cross-training method.

These are the most suitable cross-training options for your injury.

Hip/Lower Back/Glute/ Hamstring Injury

- Elliptical

- Pool Running

- Swimming (not breaststroke)

- Stair Hiking

- Walking · Weights

Knee / ITB Injury

- Elliptical

- Pool Running

- Swimming (not breaststroke)

- Uphill Treadmill Walking

- Walking

- Weights

Foot / Ankle / Shin / Plantar Fascia / Calf

- Cycling

- Pool Running

- Swimming · Stair Hiking (depending on injury)

- Walking (depending on injury)

- Weights

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Injured runners often fall into unhealthy habits when they’re unable to run. Their diet tends to decline, stress levels increase, and mental health can take a hit. However, maintaining the discipline to follow a structured cross-training plan can significantly speed up recovery. Pairing this with a nutritious, wholesome diet will further enhance the healing process. I encourage you to embrace the “Just Eat Real Food” (JERF) approach while following this cross training plan to support your recovery and overall well-being.

Week 1: “Just Eat Real Food” (JERF) Principle

Focus: Reintroduce a whole-food-based diet, reduce inflammation, and prioritize nutrient density. No strict counting of macronutrients, just focus on food quality.

Key Strategies:

- Eliminate processed foods : Avoid packaged snacks, refined sugars, and artificial ingredients.

- Anti-inflammatory focus : Include foods rich in omega-3s (e.g., fatty fish, chia seeds), turmeric, ginger, and colourful fruits/vegetables.

- Hydration : Aim for 2.5-3L of water daily, and include herbal teas or water infused with lemon/cucumber.

Sample Day in Detail:

- Breakfast : Spinach and mushroom omelet (2-3 eggs) cooked in olive oil, served with ½ avocado and a side of fresh berries (blueberries or raspberries).

- Morning Snack : Sliced apple with 1-2 tablespoons of almond butter.

- Lunch : Grilled chicken breast with roasted sweet potatoes, steamed green beans, and a mixed greens salad topped with olive oil and balsamic vinegar.

- Afternoon Snack : A small handful of raw walnuts and a hard-boiled egg.

- Dinner : Baked salmon with quinoa and roasted Brussels sprouts. Sprinkle with turmeric and black pepper for anti-inflammatory benefits.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week two of our 4 week Cross Training Plan for Injured Runners

I hope your first week on the plan went well and you have found a variety of cross training methods that you enjoy. Remember that it is best to use as many different cross-training methods as possible. Using a variety of muscle groups will aid your recovery and reduce repetition. For example, it would generally be safer on your body for you to do 30 minutes of pool running and 30 minutes of cycling, rather than a straight 60 minutes of cycling.

This week we are increasing the duration of the cross training sessions, and continuing to work on flexibility, mobility and strength.

How much time can you train for?

Your overall volume of cross-training should be matched to your current level of running fitness. For example, If you usually do 3 x 5km runs / week and this adds up to 90 minutes of total training time, then your total cross-training volume for the first week should be 90 – 120 minutes total.

Because cross-training is lower impact and easier on your body than running, you can add approximately 25% to your current total weekly time volume to get a rough equivalent training effect.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Week 2: Balanced Macronutrient Ratios

Focus: Meet energy needs for cross-training by balancing macronutrients. Start considering portion sizes and ensuring the right fuel balance.

Macro Targets:

- Carbs : 45-55%

- Protein : 20-25%

- Fats : 25-30%

Key Strategies:

- Fuel before and after workouts : Prioritise carbs and protein pre/post cross-training.

- Portion awareness : Use visual cues like “palm size” for protein, “fist size” for carbs, and “thumb size” for fats.

- Slow-digesting carbs : Stick to options like brown rice, quinoa, sweet potatoes, and oats.

Sample Day in Detail:

- Breakfast : Overnight oats made with ½ cup oats, unsweetened almond milk, chia seeds, and topped with sliced banana and a sprinkle of cinnamon.

- Morning Snack : 2 boiled eggs and carrot sticks.

- Lunch : Turkey and avocado wrap using a whole-grain tortilla, filled with spinach, tomato, and hummus. Add a side of roasted sweet potato wedges.

- Afternoon Snack : Greek yogurt (unsweetened) topped with a handful of granola and fresh strawberries.

- Dinner : Grilled tofu or chicken stir-fry with mixed vegetables (bell peppers, broccoli, snap peas) and ½ cup brown rice.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week three of our 4 week Cross Training Plan for Injured Runners

We are increasing the duration of the cross training sessions again this week.

If you are already training at a level that feels right for you, and that matches your current fitness level, then stick with what you are doing. The main aim is to help you training consistently and maintain your fitness level and strength, so further increases in volume may not be necessary.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Week 3: Higher Protein Focus (For Muscle Maintenance)

Focus: Support muscle repair and recovery by increasing protein intake slightly while maintaining balanced energy levels.

Macro Targets:

- Carbs : 40-50%

- Protein : 25-30%

- Fats : 20-25%

Key Strategies:

- Protein timing : Spread protein intake evenly throughout the day (e.g., 20-30g per meal/snack).

- Recovery meals : Post-workout snacks should include both protein and carbs (e.g., protein shake + fruit).

- Lean protein choices : Incorporate options like chicken, turkey, fish, eggs, tofu, and legumes.

Sample Day in Detail:

- Breakfast : Scrambled eggs (3 eggs) with sautéed kale, mushrooms, and whole-grain toast.

- Morning Snack : Protein smoothie with whey protein, unsweetened almond milk, spinach, frozen berries, and 1 tablespoon almond butter.

- Lunch : Grilled chicken salad with mixed greens, cherry tomatoes, cucumber, and pumpkin seeds. Use a tahini-based dressing. Add ½ cup quinoa for carbs.

- Afternoon Snack : Low-fat cottage cheese (½ cup) with pineapple chunks.

- Dinner : Baked cod with ¾ cup wild rice, roasted asparagus, and a drizzle of lemon juice and olive oil.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week four of our 4 week Cross Training Plan for Injured Runners

When can you run again?

Once you are able to perform your normal daily activities with 2/10 pain or less, then you should be ready to start a gentle and progressive return to running.

You may need to repeat the 4-week cross training plan if your day-to-day pain is still more than 2/10. It will depend on the nature and severity of your injury.

During the early return to running phase, it is vital that you learn to run with good technique, continue to work on your strength and flexibility, and gradually build your volume using a progressive and frequent walk/run intervals.

You are now ready to start our Return To Running Program

This 10-week program is specifically designed to help you build volume safely and improve your running for life.

Be patient and consistent and you will be back running with better technique and a stronger body before you know it.

Please Note: Not all injuries are the same. We definitely recommend you seek medical advice before starting the program. Following the incorrect rehab exercises could delay your recovery or cause further injury. This program is a guide only and does not replace the advice of medical professionals.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Week 4: Adjusted for Recovery and Cross-Training Intensity

Focus: Tailor carb intake based on workout intensity while maintaining balanced nutrition. High-intensity cross-training may require more carbs.

Macro Targets (Adjust as needed):

- Carbs : 50-60% (if high-intensity cross-training)

- Protein : 20-25%

- Fats : 20-25%

Key Strategies:

- Increase carbs on active days : Use starchy carbs (sweet potatoes, rice, oats) for sustained energy.

- Energy-dense snacks : Incorporate nutrient-rich options like trail mix, nut butter, and smoothies.

- Continue anti-inflammatory foods : Turmeric, ginger, leafy greens, and berries remain important for recovery.

Sample Day in Detail:

- Breakfast : Whole-grain pancakes (made with oats and eggs) topped with almond butter, sliced banana, and a drizzle of maple syrup.

- Morning Snack : Small trail mix (¼ cup nuts, seeds, and dried fruit) or a small energy bar.

- Lunch : Grilled salmon power bowl with farro, steamed broccoli, and avocado slices. Add a squeeze of lime for flavour.

- Afternoon Snack : Low-fat string cheese, 1 rice cake, and a handful of grapes.

- Dinner : Lean beef or turkey stir-fry with soba noodles, sautéed vegetables (zucchini, carrots, mushrooms), and sesame oil for flavour.

glossary.definition: You can ride indoors on a stationary bike (like a spin bike at the gym), you can set your own bike up on an indoor trainer, or you can choose to ride outdoors. This includes gravel riding and mountain biking. Pick the option you enjoy the most.
Most gyms will have an elliptical trainer. Using one feels like a cross between running and cycling. They were designed to replicate the action of running but without the impact.

Pool running is running in the deep end of a swimming pool wearing a flotation belt or flotation vest. You are fully submerged in the water with only your head above the surface. You are NOT touching the floor of the pool.

Similar to uphill walking, stair hiking is a lot lower impact than running. You don’t need a gym membership, just a flight (or two) of stairs. The idea is to hike up the stairs with an upright posture driving up with your glute muscles, and walk back down again slowly to recover.

Swimming is an excellent way to improve your upper body strength and breathing control. If you have a knee or hip injury then be careful with any breaststroke swimming. Freestyle and backstroke will be better options for you

This is a lot lower impact than running, so quite a few running injuries will cope well with uphill walking. It is a great way to get your heart rate up into the beneficial AEROBIC TRAINING ZONE, and it strengthens your calf and glute muscles in a very running-specific way.

There is a lot to be said for just getting some time on your feet. Generally speaking, the more you move the better it is for your body. Flat walking won’t get your heart rate up like uphill treadmill walking or stair hiking, but it will still help you to preserve a lot of your fitness and strength. It is MUCH better for your mind and body than complete rest.

Working on your upper body, core and leg strength will help you to maintain your fitness and should help with your running form when you return to running. There will be a lot of lower body exercises you can perform which don’t aggravate your particular injury. As a general rule of thumb – if any particular exercise feels like it is aggravating your injury, then don’t do it.
